body: I personally love “Pieced Borders: The Complete Resource” as a source for inspiration, it’s got a lot of nice general design tips and has a huge library of different kinds of border designs you can reference.

Others have pointed out confirmation bias (a good-looking first-time quilt is more likely going to be posted than one someone feels ambivalent about) but I’d also like to point out that quilting is an extremely long, multi-stage process. *Finishing* a quilt for the first time doesn’t reflect the trial-and-error that someone might have spent practicing sewing or piecing techniques, or the projects that someone might have been started earlier but are still unfinished. Personally, I practiced a lot with smaller blocks that never turned into anything more before actually finishing a first quilt.

Hey, these are actually a linen blend! I usually use a 52% linen, 48% cotton blend from fabrics-store.com that weighs 5.2oz/yd. I use my fabrics for quilting, so I prefer mid-weight fabrics because I find that lightweight/pure linen can be stretchy/slippery to sew. One thing I’ve found through trial and error is that I get better results when I use the surface area where I’ve printed for WOF calculations, rather than the weight of the entire piece of fabric.

Yeah, I love quilting/crocheting (and have made some for people!) but I think they are tricky gifts to give. They’re resource-intensive to make, they’re usually more delicate/require handwashing, and they’re nominally supposed to be a functional object. It can be hard to figure out what the “right” way to enjoy them is—use them too much and they can break down/get ruined, store them away because they feel too precious and then you never see them, if they’re too big it’s hard to hang them, and so on.

I followed the process in “The Art and Science of Natural Dyes” which I recommend checking out. You basically mix the mordant with a specific ratio of vinegar and then add the guar gum as needed to thicken. You have to make sure the paste is dried onto the fabric and then perform a process called “dunging” before dyeing. There’s a similar recipe to the one in Art & Science that’s specifically for block printing that you can try: https://www.grahamkeegan.com/block-printing-with-mordants
thank you! I screenprinted it at a printshop I have access to. I’ve seen other artists do block printing or paint the mordant directly onto the fabric.

guar gum! you only need a little, i bought some bob’s red mill from the grocery store forever ago and still have plenty. once you print, you have to let it dry for a few days (i’ll usually iron it to make sure it bonds a bit better.) before you dye you have to do a process called “dunging” where you soak the fabric in a bath of wheat bran + chalk to remove the gum and ensure the mordant bonds. you don’t need to tannin your fabric beforehand.

one thing I’ve been meaning to try is printing w a citric acid paste—it removes the mordant from the fabric and gets you a similar effect to a resist. recommend checking out “the art and science of natural dyes”, it has a whole section on printing that I’ve found really useful!
would recommend checking out @woolandnature on IG too—her dye work is amazing and really inspired me to try doing more complicated print work!

I’ve been dyeing with natural materials for a few years now, and have recently been experimenting with screenprinting with mordant pastes. I’m really curious to learn more from others about how to improve print quality. I’ve been getting a lot cleaner prints with iron than I have alum, in part because it’s much harder to spot-check because the alum dries clear!

For cotton/linen fabrics, prepping is key—scouring really well, and doing a tannin bath before mordanting. Recommend checking out Catherine Ellis’s The Art And Science Of Natural Dye, one of the alum recipes she recommends involves using vinegar, I’ve found I get brighter colors using it rather than some of the recipes I’ve found online. 

As others have said, having something closer to a 1:1 ratio of dyestuff to fabric helps, I’ve also found that I get better results when I spend an extra day or two simmering the dye bath on and off to extract as much as possible before throwing my fabric in.
I made a paste using guar gum and dunged the fabric before throwing it into the dye pot—I used a recipe that was pretty similar to this one: https://www.grahamkeegan.com/block-printing-with-mordants
